title: Four women in the family tree (Matthew 1:1–17)
hook: a birthday photo with someone cropped out: why would Jesus' family tree keep the names a tidy one would cut?
tomorrow: Joseph's mind is made up. then he falls asleep…

segments.voice: Year four closed on a promise to frightened friends, a house with many rooms: there is room for you. Year five opens on a page full of names.
screen: `THERE IS ROOM FOR YOU.` → `YEAR FIVE: A PAGE OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: A birthday post in the family group chat: an old photo, everyone squeezed onto one porch. Look closer, and someone at the edge has been cropped out. Families keep a tidy version of themselves, the one that gets framed. This year reads one Gospel straight through, Matthew, from page one, and page one is a family tree. "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob." Father after father, the easy page to skim. Then, four times before Mary, the pattern breaks, and in walks a name a tidy version would cut. So, one question for today: why keep them?
screen: `SOMEONE CROPPED OUT AT THE EDGE.` → `ABRAHAM BEGAT ISAAC.` → `WHY KEEP THE HARD NAMES?`

segments.voice: Matthew opens: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham." A genealogy says who you are by saying whose you are. "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar": Tamar, a widow wronged by her father-in-law Judah, who in the end admits, "She hath been more righteous than I." "Salmon begat Booz of Rachab": Rahab of Jericho, who hid two spies on her roof. "Booz begat Obed of Ruth": Ruth the Moabitess, a foreigner. And one woman Matthew never names: "her that had been the wife of Urias." That's Bathsheba, known here only by the husband King David sent to his death. Matthew never says why these four. Some readers notice outsiders; some notice women wronged by powerful men; some notice women who acted when the men around them failed. The answer the page gives either way: the line keeps the hard stories, by name. Ruth is shared ground with a neighbor. Jewish tradition reads her book aloud at the festival of Shavuot, and it ends on a family line too, in the Jewish Publication Society's translation: "he is the father of Jesse, the father of David." An old midrash on Ruth says the book was written to teach how great the reward is for acts of kindness. Both traditions honor the foreign widow who chose to stay. And one honest difference: the Book of Ruth ends its line at David. Matthew carries it on to Jesus, whom Christians call the son of David.
screen: `THE BOOK OF THE GENERATION.` · `TAMAR, RAHAB, RUTH, THE WIFE OF URIAS.` · `RUTH, READ AT SHAVUOT.` · `THE LINE ENDS AT DAVID, OR GOES ON.` · then, large: `EVERY NAME COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Find a scrap of paper and write two names from your own family tree, by blood or by choice, that a tidy version would leave off: the outsider, the one who was wronged, the one with the complicated story. Then rest with the paper in front of you. If you pray, you can hold those names before God; if not, let them simply be counted.
Genealogy. A family line, name after name. Matthew's opens his Gospel, and stops four times for women with hard stories.
Your line: every name counts. Even the one Matthew never said out loud. Year five, day one.

howItsDone: Some churches read the genealogy from Matthew 1 aloud near Christmas, every name included, and some Christians read a Gospel straight through, a chapter at a time.

Thamar.meaning: the King James spelling of Tamar, Judah's daughter-in-law

Moabitess.meaning: a woman from Moab, a land outside Israel

Urias.meaning: the King James spelling of Uriah, Bathsheba's husband

Shavuot.meaning: a Jewish festival when the Book of Ruth is read

midrash.meaning: an old Jewish teaching that reads and explains scripture

notes: Year five opener (Block A, Matthew read through). The hook's 'four times before Mary' counts Thamar, Rachab, Ruth and 'her that had been the wife of Urias' (Matthew 1:3, 1:5, 1:6); Mary follows at 1:16. Confirm.

Three readings of why the women appear (outsiders; wrongs done by powerful men; women who acted when men failed) are offered as 'some readers' without ranking. Tamar is not called a foreigner here, since Genesis doesn't say. Confirm the framing of Bathsheba is fair: she is described as wronged by David, not as a sinner.
Rahab hid the spies 'on her roof' (Joshua 2:6).
original: γένεσις for Matthew 1:1 (biblos geneseos); confirm the note.
Matthew 1:17 (the generations counted in three sets) is deliberately left out, under the claims rule.

Recipe v3, wisdom shape. Question: why keep the hard names? Answer: Matthew's line keeps them by name. Unity thread: Ruth, honored in Jewish tradition (read at Shavuot; Ruth 4:17 ends the line at David, quoted from JPS 1917; Ruth Rabbah 2:14, Rabbi Zeira, paraphrased: the book teaches the reward for acts of kindness). Honest difference: Ruth's book ends the line at David; Matthew carries it to Jesus, whom Christians call the son of David. No ranking. A Judaism Keeper should confirm the JPS 1917 wording of Ruth 4:17, the Ruth Rabbah attribution, and that the 'honest difference' line reads fairly to a Jewish reader.
